{{short description|American thermodynamicist}}
'''Grant McDonald Wilson''' (May 24, 1931 – September 10, 2012) was a notable American [[thermodynamics|thermodynamicist]].  He is widely known to the fields of [[chemical engineering]] and [[physical chemistry]] for having developed the [[Wilson equation]], one of the first attempts of [[engineering|practical importance]] to [[chemical process modeling|model]] [[azeotrope|nonideal]] behavior in liquid mixtures as observed in practice with common polar [[chemical compounds|compounds]] such as [[alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]]s, [[amine]]s, etc.  The equation has been in use in all commercial [[process simulation|chemical process simulators]] to predict [[vapor-liquid equilibrium|phase behavior]] and produce safe [[process design]]s of [[industrial process|commercial]] and [[environmental protection]] importance to the [[chemical industry]].<ref> R. V. Orye and J. M. Prausnitz, “MULTICOMPONENT EQUILIBRIA—THE WILSON EQUATION”, [[Industrial & Engineering Chemistry]], 57(5):18–26, 1965</ref>  He founded the company Wilco (now Wiltec) in 1977 to research, measure, commercialize, and publish [[physical property|thermophysical property]] data for numerous chemical mixtures of interest to the industry.<ref>Preface to the Memorial Edition for Grant M. Wilson, [[Journal of Chemical & Engineering Data]], 59(4):943–945, 2014</ref>  The ''[[Journal of Chemical & Engineering Data]]'' published a posthumous issue in honor of Wilson in April 2014 in recognition of his contributions to the field. 

== Biography ==
Wilson was born in Colonia Pacheco, [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]] (one of the [[Mormon colonies in Mexico]]). He did his undergraduate work at BYU in 1953 and then attended and graduated from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) with a [[PhD]] in [[physical chemistry]] in 1957.

While at MIT he began his career by developing one of the first computer-based [[activity coefficient]] equations.<ref>Wilson, Grant McDonald, Vapor-Liquid Equilibria From Measurements of Pressure, Temperature and Over-All Composition. The System Water - 2-Butoxyethanol, Ph.D. Thesis, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 1958.</ref><ref>Wilson, Grant M., "Vapor–Liquid Equilibrium. XI. A New Expression for the Excess Free Energy of Mixing," [[Journal of the American Chemical Society]], 86:127-130, 1964.</ref> Known as the Wilson Equation,<ref>Walas, Stanley M., (1985) ''[[Phase Equilibria]] in Chemical Engineering'', Boston: Butterworth, pp. 192-201. {{ISBN|0-409-95162-5}}</ref> it is one of the most widely used equations in the field of industrial [[thermodynamics]] for the prediction of phase equilibria.

Wilson has been a [[research scientist]] measuring and reporting physical properties and [[phase equilibria]] data for most of his career. He joined Shell Research and Development in California upon graduating from MIT, he then joined Air Products and later moved to PVT Inc. of Houston, Texas. While there he performed a number of Research Projects for the [[Gas Processors Association]]. At this time he also did work with cubic equations of state (EOS), he was one of the first to modify the alpha form of the Redlich-Kwong EOS to better represent pure component [[vapor pressure]]s.<ref>Wilson, G. M., "Vapor Liquid Equilibria, Correlation By Means Of A Modified Redlich-Kwong Equation Of State," Adv. Cryog. Eng., 9: 168-176, 1964.</ref> 

He next taught at [[BYU]] in Provo, Utah, from 1970 to 1978 while there he was a part of the on-campus research group, the Thermochemical Institute founded by Profs. James J. Christensen and [[Reed M. Izatt]]. Wilson left BYU to create the company [[Wilco]] (now [https://www.wiltecresearch.com/ Wiltec]) Research Company in 1977 which measured data for the Chemical Process Industries (CPI).<ref>{{cite journal |journal= BYU Magazine |url= http://magazine.byu.edu/?act=view&a=566 |title= SEVEN HONORED WITH BYU EMERITUS AWARDS |first= Charlene R. |last= Winters |date= Summer 2001 |accessdate= 2013-08-18 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110517221850/http://magazine.byu.edu/?act=view&a=566 |archive-date= 2011-05-17 |url-status= live }}</ref>

The Wilson equation was published by Grant M. Wilson as "[[Vapor–liquid equilibrium|Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium]]. XI. A New Expression for the Excess Free Energy of Mixing" in the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]'' 86:127-130, 1964.<ref>{{cite web |last= M. Wilson |first= Grant |title= The Wilson Equation |url= http://www.trentfguidry.net/post/2010/03/27/Wilson-equation-activity-coefficients.aspx |accessdate= 16 October 2011 |url-status= dead |archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20111014033053/http://www.trentfguidry.net/post/2010/03/27/Wilson-equation-activity-coefficients.aspx |archivedate= 14 October 2011 }}</ref>

Wilson and his wife, Reta Raphiel were married in the [[Logan Temple]] on September 18, 1950. Together in 2002, they served as [[Mormon missionaries|missionaries]] for [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] in [[Bangalore]], India for two years.

Wilson died on September 10, 2012, in Orem, Utah.
